claims.source: Although eCB modulation of voltage-dependent Ca2+ and K+ conductances, typically resulting in the downregulation of neurotransmitter release, has been demonstrated at multiple stages of retinal processing from photoreceptors to retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Fan and Yazulla, 2003; Lalonde et al., 2006; Middleton and Protti, 2011; Yazulla et al., 2000), these observations have not been directly linked to specific perceptual outcomes.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Cannabis consumption in humans has been reported to positively modulate contrast discrimination.
claims.source: On the other hand, cannabis consumption in humans has been reported to positively modulate contrast discrimination (Russo et al., 2004; West, 1991).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: CB1R is present in the brain of adult Xenopus laevis frogs.
claims.source: The presence of CB1Rs has been reported in the brain of the adult Xenopus laevis frog (Cesa et al., 2001; Cottone et al., 2003) and in the tadpole olfactory bulb (Breunig et al., 2010; Czesnik et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: CB1R immunoreactivity is present in the outer and inner plexiform layers of Xenopus tadpole retinae.
claims.source: We examined the retinae of Xenopus tadpoles, and found intense CB1R immunoreactivity (CB1R-IR) in the outer and inner plexiform layers (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with reports in other species (Middleton and Protti, 2011; Yazulla et al., 2000; Zabouri et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Somatic CB1R immunoreactivity has been described in RGCs of salamander and chick but not in rat.
claims.source: Somatic CB1R-IR has been described in the RGCs of salamander and chick (Straiker et al., 1999), but not in rat (Yazulla et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: CB1R immunoreactivity is associated with GFP-positive RGCs in Isl2b:GFP transgenic frogs.
claims.source: Using Isl2b:GFP transgenic frogs, in which expression of green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the retina is restricted to RGCs, we found CB1R-IR associated with GFP-positive RGCs in histological sections (Figure 1c) and in overnight dissociated retinal cultures (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 application increased RGC spiking rates in response to full field light-ON stimuli.
claims.source: Extracellular multi-unit recordings in isolated eye preparations (Figure 2a) revealed that application of the CB1R agonist WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM) increased spiking rates of RGCs in response to both full field light-ON (before: 34.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 43.3 ± 4.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.010, two-way RM ANOVA) and light-OFF (before: 37.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 45.2 ± 4.2 Hz, n = 10, p=0.011) stimuli (Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 application increased RGC spiking rates in response to full field light-OFF stimuli.
claims.source: Extracellular multi-unit recordings in isolated eye preparations (Figure 2a) revealed that application of the CB1R agonist WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM) increased spiking rates of RGCs in response to both full field light-ON (before: 34.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 43.3 ± 4.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.010, two-way RM ANOVA) and light-OFF (before: 37.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 45.2 ± 4.2 Hz, n = 10, p=0.011) stimuli (Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: ACEA enhanced RGC spiking to light-OFF stimuli.
claims.source: This cannabinoid-mediated enhancement of evoked RGC responses was confirmed using a different CB1R agonist arachidonyl-2'-chloroethylamide (ACEA, 1 µM) which gave a similar enhancement of spiking to light-OFF stimuli (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,e; before: 30.5 ± 4.1 Hz, after: 40.0 ± 6.0 Hz, n = 10, p=0.033).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON stimulation.
claims.source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-OFF stimulation.
claims.source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
claims.source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the URB597 experimental results.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 perfusion did not produce significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in ERG recordings.
claims.source: However, perfusion of WIN 55,212-2 did not produce any significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in response to step increments or decrements of light (Figure 2g, n = 6, 6, 6, 6; p=0.78, 0.79, 0.89, 0.68, two-way RM ANOVA), suggesting that CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina, consistent with a recent report in the mouse (Cécyre et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ERG recording data shown in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina.
claims.source: However, perfusion of WIN 55,212-2 did not produce any significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in response to step increments or decrements of light (Figure 2g, n = 6, 6, 6, 6; p=0.78, 0.79, 0.89, 0.68, two-way RM ANOVA), suggesting that CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina, consistent with a recent report in the mouse (Cécyre et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data and supported by citation to prior study.

claims.claim: CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to light-ON stimulation.
claims.source: Comparing average peak Ca2+ transients evoked by full-field light-ON and light-OFF stimulation before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3c), we found that CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to visual stimulation, but instead decreased it in the case of light-OFF stimulation (Figure 3d,e, ON: n = 10, p=0.17, OFF: n = 10, p=0.002), consistent with reports from salamander of a CB1R-mediated reduction of the L-type Ca2+ current12.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CB1R activation decreased bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to light-OFF stimulation.
claims.source: Comparing average peak Ca2+ transients evoked by full-field light-ON and light-OFF stimulation before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3c), we found that CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to visual stimulation, but instead decreased it in the case of light-OFF stimulation (Figure 3d,e, ON: n = 10, p=0.17, OFF: n = 10, p=0.002), consistent with reports from salamander of a CB1R-mediated reduction of the L-type Ca2+ current12.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Peak Ca2+ transients in amacrine cell terminals evoked by light-ON and light-OFF stimulation were not significantly different before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion.
claims.source: Peak Ca2+ transients in amacrine cell terminals evoked by light-ON and light-OFF stimulation were not significantly different before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3f–i, ON: n = 10, p=0.36; OFF: n = 10, p=0.48).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Application of WIN 55,212-2 resulted in a significant decrease in the total integrated EPSC in RGCs.
claims.source: Application of WIN 55,212-2 resulted in a significant decrease in the total integrated EPSC, measured over 1 s following stimulus onset (Figure 3m,n, n = 7, p=0.025, two-way RM ANOVA, before vs. +WIN simple effect).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2.
claims.source: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 3o, n = 5, p=0.199, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak posthoc test) but a decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed (Figure 3p, n = 5, p=0.029).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: A decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed with WIN 55,212-2.
claims.source: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 3o, n = 5, p=0.199, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak posthoc test) but a decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed (Figure 3p, n = 5, p=0.029).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: AM-251 pretreatment completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 on RGC firing.
claims.source: Pretreatment with the CB1R blocker AM-251 (5 µM) completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 4a, n = 10, p=0.487, one-tailed one-way RM ANOVA) or ACEA (Figure 4b, n = 10, p=0.360) on RGC firing, further underscoring the requirement for CB1R activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: AM-251 pretreatment prevented the potentiating effects of ACEA on RGC firing.
claims.source: Pretreatment with the CB1R blocker AM-251 (5 µM) completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 4a, n = 10, p=0.487, one-tailed one-way RM ANOVA) or ACEA (Figure 4b, n = 10, p=0.360) on RGC firing, further underscoring the requirement for CB1R activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: AM-251 prevented the enhancement caused by elevating endogenous AEA using URB597.
claims.source: The enhancement produced by elevating endogenous AEA using URB597 (Figure 2e) was also prevented by AM-251 (Figure 4c, n = 10, p=0.500).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: Gabazine did not prevent the WIN 55,212-2-induced increase in RGC firing in response to light.
claims.source: The selective GABA-A receptor blocker gabazine (6 µM) had no specific effect on visually-evoked spike rates and did not prevent the WIN 55,212-2-induced increase in RGC firing in response to light (Figure 4d, n = 10, p=0.012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: Strychnine prevented the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
claims.source: However, strychnine (60 µM), a potent and selective antagonist of glycine receptors (GlyRs) prevented (Figure 4e, n = 10, p=0.423) and reversed (Figure 4f, n = 10, p=0.044) the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4e and 4f.

claims.claim: Strychnine reversed the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
claims.source: However, strychnine (60 µM), a potent and selective antagonist of glycine receptors (GlyRs) prevented (Figure 4e, n = 10, p=0.423) and reversed (Figure 4f, n = 10, p=0.044) the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: Both CB1Rs and GlyRs are required for the cannabinoid-mediated increase in RGC response to visual stimulation.
claims.source: These results show that both CB1Rs and GlyRs are required for the cannabinoid-mediated increase in RGC response to visual stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological experiments with AM-251 and strychnine.

claims.claim: NKCC1 and KCC2 mRNAs are expressed in stage 45 Xenopus retina.
claims.source: NKCC1 and KCC2 are co-expressed in RGCs in fish retina (Dmitriev et al., 2007), and we were able to detect both mRNAs in stage 45 Xenopus retina (Figure 4i).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4i.

claims.claim: Perfusion of bumetanide alone was sufficient to increase the firing rates of RGCs in response to light.
claims.source: Perfusion of the selective NKCC1 inhibitor bumetanide (10 µM) alone was sufficient to increase the firing rates of RGCs in response to light, mimicking the effect of CB1R activation (Figure 4g, n = 10, p=0.025).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4g.

claims.claim: Subsequent addition of WIN 55,212-2 in the presence of bumetanide produced no additional increase in RGC firing rate.
claims.source: Subsequent addition of WIN 55,212-2 in the presence of bumetanide produced no additional increase in RGC firing rate (n = 10, p=0.224).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 application occluded the increase in RGC firing rate produced by adding bumetanide.
claims.source: Furthermore, WIN 55,212-2 application (Figure 4h, n = 9, p=0.012) occluded the increase in RGC firing rate produced by adding bumetanide (Figure 4h, n = 9, p=0.224 vs. WIN alone).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4h.

claims.claim: CB1R activation may work by regulating NKCC1 function to modulate the driving force of chloride currents in RGCs.
claims.source: These results argue that CB1R activation may work by regulating NKCC1 function to modulate the driving force of chloride currents in RGCs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the bumetanide occlusion experiments.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1.
claims.source: We examined the involvement of these regulatory molecules by performing western blotting on retina homogenates from animals treated with WIN 55,212-2. WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1, indicating its activation downstream of the CB1R (Figure 4j,k); however, this was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4j and 4k.

claims.claim: WIN 55,212-2 application was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217.
claims.source: We examined the involvement of these regulatory molecules by performing western blotting on retina homogenates from animals treated with WIN 55,212-2. WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1, indicating its activation downstream of the CB1R (Figure 4j,k); however, this was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claims.claim: Dorsomorphin reversed the effects of WIN 55,212-2, reducing RGC spiking rate in response to light-OFF flashes.
claims.source: We found that dorsomorphin (10 µM) reversed the effects of WIN 55,212-2, reducing RGCs spiking rate in response to light-OFF flashes (before: 37.5 ± 6.3 Hz, after: 22.9 ± 2.6 Hz, Figure 4l, n = 10, p=0.0095, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4l.

claims.claim: CB1R signaling inhibits NKCC1 through the activation of AMPK.
claims.source: These results indicate that CB1R signaling inhibits NKCC1 through the activation of AMPK.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the dorsomorphin experiment.

claims.claim: CB1R activation consistently caused a rapid decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs indicating a reduction in [Cl−]i.
claims.source: In all experiments, CB1R activation consistently caused a rapid decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs (Figure 5d,e, n = 15 cells, p=0.001, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post-test) indicating a reduction in [Cl−]i.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: No FRET changes in amacrine, bipolar or Müller glia cell types were detected with CB1R activation.
claims.source: No FRET changes in amacrine (n = 16, p=0.649), bipolar (n = 12, p=0.972) or Müller glia (n = 8, p=0.997) cell types were detected (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: The decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs was not observed when expressing a control Cl−-insensitive Clomeleon-M69Q construct.
claims.source: The decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs was not observed when expressing a control Cl−-insensitive Clomeleon-M69Q construct (Figure 5f, n = 5, p=0.996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with AM-251 prevented changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2.
claims.source: Pretreatment with AM-251 (n = 8) or bumetanide (n = 9) prevented any changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 5f, p=0.996 for both).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with bumetanide prevented changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2.
claims.source: Pretreatment with AM-251 (n = 8) or bumetanide (n = 9) prevented any changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 5f, p=0.996 for both).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: CB1R activation induces a RGC-specific decrease in [Cl−]i by regulating NKCC1 activity.
claims.source: These data suggest that CB1R activation induces a RGC-specific decrease in [Cl−]i by regulating NKCC1 activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Clomeleon imaging experiments.

claims.claim: With synaptic block, WIN 55,212-2 application still significantly decreased the cyan:yellow ratio in RGCs.
claims.source: To determine if synaptic activity might contribute to the changes in [Cl−]i, we blocked synaptic transmission with a cocktail of DNQX (20 µM), AP4 (50 µM), picrotoxin (100 µM), strychnine (60 µM) and TTX (1 µM). With synaptic block, WIN 55,212-2 application still significantly decreased the cyan:yellow ratio in RGCs (Figure 5g, n = 14, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5g.

claims.claim: Retinal CB1R activation rapidly decreases [Cl−]i specifically in RGCs through a NKCC1-dependent and neurotransmission-independent mechanism.
claims.source: These data indicate that retinal CB1R activation rapidly decreases [Cl−]i specifically in RGCs through a NKCC1-dependent and neurotransmission-independent mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the synaptic block experiments.

claims.claim: A small but significant leftward shift for EGly could be seen following wash-on of WIN 55,212-2.
claims.source: We measured EGly by generating current-voltage (I-V) plots of peak current evoked by a brief application of glycine (500 µM for 20 ms) over a range of holding potentials (Figure 6e). A small but significant leftward shift for EGly could be seen following wash-on of WIN 55,212-2 in the bath (∆V = −3.2 ± 0.8 mV, n = 7, p=0.008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Inhibition of NKCC1 with bath application of bumetanide produced a similar shift in EGly.
claims.source: Inhibition of NKCC1 with bath application of bumetanide produced a similar shift in EGly (Figure 6f, ∆V = −1.6 ± 0.5 mV, n = 5, p=0.026).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: Application of WIN 55,212-2 significantly hyperpolarized RGCs in dissociated cultures.
claims.source: Application of WIN 55,212-2 significantly hyperpolarized RGCs (Figure 6h, uncorrected for liquid junction potential; n = 6, p=0.004, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gramicidin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 6h.

claims.claim: The WIN 55,212-2-induced hyperpolarization was prevented in the presence of AM-251.
claims.source: This shift was prevented in the presence of AM-251 (Figure 6i, n = 6, p=0.14, one-way RM ANOVA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gramicidin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 6i.

claims.claim: CB1R-mediated hyperpolarization does not depend on cannabinoid actions on other cells in the retina.
claims.source: This experiment not only confirms that CB1R activation can hyperpolarize RGCs, but the fact that it does so in isolated cells, shows that this effect does not depend on cannabinoid actions on other cells in the retina.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the dissociated cell experiments.

claims.claim: RGCs decrease their excitability following a period of depolarization and firing through the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
claims.source: RGCs are known to decrease their excitability following a period of depolarization and firing through the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels as a way of extending their dynamic range (Kim and Rieke, 2001, 2003; Weick and Demb, 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses.
claims.source: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses, whereas it decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses (Figure 6k).
claims.evidence: This is supported by current clamp recording data shown in Figure 6k.

claims.claim: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses.
claims.source: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses, whereas it decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses (Figure 6k).
claims.evidence: This is supported by current clamp recording data shown in Figure 6k.

claims.claim: eCBs can be released from neurons in response to stimulation driving a prolonged increase in intracellular Ca2+.
claims.source: eCBs can be released from neurons in response to stimulation driving a prolonged increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Hashimotodani et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claims.claim: Sustained peripheral illumination elevated the RGC spike rate evoked by light-OFF test stimuli in the central subfield.
claims.source: In a significant majority of cases, sustained peripheral illumination elevated the RGC spike rate evoked by light-OFF test stimuli in the central subfield (Figure 7e, before: 4.2 ± 1.6 Hz, after: 8.8 ± 2.4 Hz, n = 10, p=0.042, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 7e.

claims.claim: The effects of conditioning stimulation were prevented by bath application of AM-251.
claims.source: Furthermore, the effects of conditioning stimulation were prevented by bath application of AM-251 (before: 6.9 ± 2.8 Hz, after: 4.7 ± 1.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.244) (Figure 7b,d,f), consistent with a CB1R-dependent mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Conditioning with peripheral field stimulation induced a CB1R-dependent decrease of [Cl−]i in RGCs.
claims.source: As predicted by our model, conditioning with peripheral field stimulation also induced a CB1R-dependent decrease of [Cl−]i in RGCs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging experiments.

claims.claim: A significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline was observed in RGCs in response to conditioning stimulation.
claims.source: In response, we observed a significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline in RGCs (Figure 7i, n = 22, p=0.0004, two-way RM ANOVA), and this effect was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251 (Figure 7j, n = 17, p=0.903).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7i.

claims.claim: The conditioning-induced reduction in [Cl−]i in RGCs was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251.
claims.source: In response, we observed a significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline in RGCs (Figure 7i, n = 22, p=0.0004, two-way RM ANOVA), and this effect was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251 (Figure 7j, n = 17, p=0.903).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7j.

claims.claim: No significant reduction in [Cl−]i was found in amacrine or bipolar cells immediately following the conditioning stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, we did not find any significant reduction in [Cl−]i in amacrine (n = 19, p=0.903) or bipolar (n = 10, p=0.831) cells immediately following the conditioning stimulation (Figure 7k).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7k.

claims.claim: CB1R activation can occur naturally in the retina in response to sustained illumination in peripheral visual fields.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that CB1R activation can occur naturally in the retina in response to sustained illumination in peripheral visual fields, and it appears to increase the number of RGCs responding to test stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conditioning stimulation experiments.

claims.claim: Following bath application of WIN 55,212-2, peak amplitudes of retinal evoked EPSCs were significantly increased.
claims.source: Direct electrical stimulation of RGCs through a glass-stimulating electrode placed in the ganglion cell layer of the eye (Figure 8a) evoked α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor-mediated retinotectal currents with latencies of about 5 ms in postsynaptic tectal neurons clamped at −60 mV. Following bath application (perfusion over the entire tadpole) of WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM), peak amplitudes of retinal evoked EPSCs were significantly increased (Figure 8b,c; 151.9 ± 17.5% baseline, n = 11, p=0.0004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The increase in EPSC amplitude was dependent on CB1R activation, as it was blocked by AM-251.
claims.source: This increase in EPSC amplitude was dependent on CB1R activation, as it was blocked by the inverse agonist AM-251 (Figure 8c, n = 5, p=0.497).
claims.evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: Increasing the endogenous AEA concentration with URB597 increased EPSC amplitude.
claims.source: Increasing the endogenous AEA concentration with URB597 similarly increased EPSC amplitude (Figure 8c, n = 7, p=0.029).
claims.evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: Treatments with NAM or JZL184 showed no enhancement of EPSC amplitude.
claims.source: Treatments with either N-arachidonyl maleimide (NAM, 150 nM, n = 7, p=0.988) or JZL184 (100 nM, n = 7, p=0.999), two selective inhibitors of monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), the 2-AG degrading enzyme, showed no enhancement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a), providing further evidence that AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
claims.source: Treatments with either N-arachidonyl maleimide (NAM, 150 nM, n = 7, p=0.988) or JZL184 (100 nM, n = 7, p=0.999), two selective inhibitors of monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), the 2-AG degrading enzyme, showed no enhancement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a), providing further evidence that AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of MAGL inhibitors.

claims.claim: The WIN 55,212-2-induced enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitudes were blocked by strychnine and bumetanide.

results.result: CB1R immunoreactivity is present in the Xenopus tadpole retina, specifically in the outer and inner plexiform layers and associated with retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in Isl2b:GFP transgenic animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C12 are supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1, with appropriate controls using transgenic animals expressing GFP specifically in RGCs. The findings are consistent with prior reports in other species (C10 cites appropriate literature), providing convergent evidence for CB1R expression in the tadpole retina.

results.result: CB1R activation by agonists WIN 55,212-2 and ACEA, or elevation of endogenous anandamide (AEA) by URB597, increases RGC spiking rates in response to light-ON and light-OFF stimuli in isolated eye preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are supported by extracellular multi-unit recordings with appropriate statistical tests (two-way RM ANOVA, n=10 per condition, p<0.05). The use of multiple CB1R agonists and the FAAH inhibitor URB597 provides converging pharmacological evidence. Sample sizes appear adequate and statistical methods are appropriate for the experimental design.

results.result: CB1R activation does not significantly affect electroretinogram (ERG) components (a-wave, b-wave, d-wave), suggesting no impact on light-evoked activity in the outer retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by ERG recordings (Figure 2g) with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way RM ANOVA, n=6 per condition, all p>0.68). The lack of effect on outer retinal responses helps localize the site of CB1R action and is consistent with prior mouse studies (C20 cites Cécyre et al., 2013).

results.result: CB1R activation decreases bipolar cell axon terminal Ca2+ transients in response to light-OFF stimulation but does not affect light-ON responses or amacrine cell terminal Ca2+ transients.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by in vivo GCaMP6s imaging data (Figure 3) with appropriate statistical analysis (n=10 terminals per condition). The selective effect on bipolar OFF responses is consistent with prior salamander studies. However, the manuscript does not clearly specify whether these are biological or technical replicates, and the number of animals contributing to the n=10 terminals is not stated.

results.result: CB1R activation decreases total integrated excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in RGCs and reduces inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in response to light-OFF but not light-ON stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by in vivo whole-cell voltage clamp recordings (Figure 3m-p) with appropriate statistical tests. Sample sizes are modest (n=5-7) but appear adequate given the within-subjects design. The findings suggest that synaptic changes alone cannot explain the increased RGC firing, supporting the authors' hypothesis of intrinsic excitability changes.

results.result: The CB1R-mediated enhancement of RGC firing requires both CB1R activation (blocked by AM-251) and glycine receptor (GlyR) function (blocked by strychnine), but not GABA-A receptors (gabazine has no effect).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 are supported by systematic pharmacological experiments (Figure 4a-f) with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (n=10 per condition). The occlusion experiments with AM-251 and the prevention/reversal by strychnine provide strong evidence for the requirement of both CB1Rs and GlyRs. However, the p-values for some 'prevention' experiments (e.g., C27: p=0.487, C31: p=0.423) suggest no significant difference from baseline, which is the expected outcome but could be more clearly stated as 'no significant enhancement' rather than 'prevented.'

results.result: NKCC1 inhibition by bumetanide mimics and occludes the effects of CB1R activation on RGC firing, suggesting that CB1R activation works by regulating NKCC1 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by RT-PCR confirming NKCC1/KCC2 expression (C34, Figure 4i) and pharmacological occlusion experiments (C35-C37, Figure 4g-h, n=9-10). The bidirectional occlusion (bumetanide blocks WIN effect and vice versa) provides strong evidence for a shared mechanism. Statistical analysis is appropriate.

results.result: CB1R activation increases phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1 levels but not phospho-NKCC1 at T212/T217, and the AMPK inhibitor dorsomorphin reverses the effects of WIN 55,212-2, indicating that CB1R signaling inhibits NKCC1 through AMPK activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by western blot data (Figure 4j-k, n=4), but the lack of increase in phospho-NKCC1 at the canonical SPAK/OSR1 sites (T212/T217) is puzzling given the increase in phospho-SPAK/OSR1. The dorsomorphin experiment (C41-C42, n=10, p=0.0095) supports AMPK involvement, but dorsomorphin is not entirely selective for AMPK and can affect other kinases. The proposed mechanism involving AMPK-mediated NKCC1 inhibition at S77 is plausible based on prior literature (Fraser et al., 2014), but direct evidence for S77 phosphorylation is lacking (no antibody available). Additional experiments with more selective AMPK inhibitors or genetic approaches would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: CB1R activation causes a rapid, RGC-specific decrease in intracellular chloride concentration [Cl−]i, as measured by Clomeleon FRET imaging, which is prevented by AM-251 or bumetanide pretreatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by in vivo two-photon Clomeleon imaging (Figure 5) with appropriate controls including a Cl−-insensitive mutant (M69Q, C45) and pharmacological blockers (C46-C47). The cell-type specificity (RGCs but not amacrine, bipolar, or Müller glia) is well-demonstrated with adequate sample sizes (n=5-16 cells per condition). Statistical analysis is appropriate (two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post-test).

results.result: The CB1R-mediated decrease in [Cl−]i in RGCs persists when synaptic transmission is blocked, indicating a neurotransmission-independent, cell-autonomous mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by Clomeleon imaging with synaptic blockers (Figure 5g, n=14 RGCs, p<0.001). The use of a comprehensive synaptic blocker cocktail (DNQX, AP4, picrotoxin, strychnine, TTX) provides strong evidence for a direct effect on RGCs rather than an indirect effect through altered synaptic input.

results.result: CB1R activation and bumetanide treatment produce small but significant hyperpolarizing shifts in the glycine receptor reversal potential (EGly) in RGCs, consistent with reduced [Cl−]i.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by in vivo whole-cell voltage clamp recordings (Figure 6e-f) with appropriate I-V curve analysis. The shifts are small (−3.2 mV for WIN, −1.6 mV for bumetanide) but statistically significant (n=5-7, p<0.05). The authors acknowledge using conventional whole-cell recording rather than gramicidin-perforated patch due to technical difficulties, which could potentially affect [Cl−]i, but the consistency with Clomeleon data supports the findings.

results.result: CB1R activation hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential of dissociated RGCs in a CB1R-dependent manner, demonstrating a cell-autonomous effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by gramicidin-perforated patch recordings from dissociated cultured RGCs (Figure 6h-i, n=6 per condition). The use of dissociated cells (C55) provides strong evidence for a cell-autonomous mechanism. The prevention by AM-251 confirms CB1R dependence. However, the liquid junction potential correction is noted but not applied, which could affect the absolute voltage values reported.

results.result: Hyperpolarizing pre-pulses increase the number of action potentials evoked by subsequent depolarizing test pulses in RGCs, while depolarizing pre-pulses decrease spike number.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by current clamp recordings (Figure 6k, n=8 cells). This result is consistent with the known phenomenon of sodium channel de-inactivation following hyperpolarization (cited as Kim and Rieke 2001, 2003; Weick and Demb 2011). The experiment provides a mechanistic link between CB1R-mediated hyperpolarization and increased RGC excitability.

results.result: Sustained peripheral illumination (conditioning stimulation) elevates RGC spike rates to central test stimuli and decreases [Cl−]i specifically in RGCs through a CB1R-dependent mechanism, suggesting physiological endocannabinoid release.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by extracellular recordings (Figure 7e, n=10, p=0.042) and Clomeleon imaging (Figure 7i-k, n=10-22 cells) showing that conditioning stimulation mimics exogenous CB1R activation. The prevention by AM-251 (C61, C64) confirms CB1R dependence. The cell-type specificity (C65) strengthens the conclusion. This result demonstrates that the mechanism can be engaged by physiological visual stimulation.

results.result: CB1R activation increases retinotectal EPSC amplitudes in tectal neurons, an effect dependent on CB1R activation and mediated by endogenous anandamide (AEA) rather than 2-AG.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recordings from tectal neurons (Figure 8b-c, n=5-11). The blockade by AM-251 (C68) and enhancement by URB597 (C69) confirm CB1R and AEA involvement. The lack of effect of MAGL inhibitors NAM and JZL184 (C70) supports AEA over 2-AG as the endogenous ligand. Statistical analysis is appropriate.

results.result: The CB1R-mediated enhancement of retinotectal EPSCs is blocked by strychnine and bumetanide, requires the presence of the eye, and is due to increased retinal excitability rather than changes at retinotectal synapses or in tectal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b) and isolated brain preparation experiments (Figure 8d, n=7, p=0.999). The lack of effect when stimulating the optic tract directly (C74) provides strong evidence that the enhancement occurs in the retina. The parallel effects of strychnine and bumetanide on RGCs and retinotectal responses (C72-C73) support a common mechanism.

results.result: CB1R activation increases tectal receptive field (RF) size and total evoked charge, likely through recruitment of initially subthreshold RGC inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by in vivo receptive field mapping experiments (Figure 8f-h, n=5, p<0.05). The increases in RF size (127.6% of baseline) and total charge (140.3% of baseline) are consistent with recruitment of additional RGC inputs. However, the sample size is modest (n=5), and the interpretation of 'recruitment of subthreshold inputs' (C78) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: CB1R activation markedly improves visual contrast sensitivity under mesopic (low-light) but not photopic conditions in freely swimming tadpoles, as measured by a dot avoidance assay, with endogenous AEA mediating this effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 are supported by behavioral tracking experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 8i-n, n=24 per group). The lack of effect under photopic conditions (C81) but dramatic improvement under mesopic conditions (C83) strongly argues for a retinal site of action (C87). The enhancement by URB597 and blockade by AM-251 (C84-C85) confirm endogenous AEA involvement. The increased escape velocity (C80) is noted as a caveat indicating effects beyond the retina. Statistical analysis is appropriate with correction for multiple comparisons.

results.result: The overall mechanism by which CB1R activation enhances visual responses involves AMPK-dependent NKCC1 inhibition, reduced [Cl−]i, hyperpolarization via enhanced GlyR-mediated Cl− currents, increased intrinsic RGC excitability through sodium channel de-inactivation, and recruitment of additional RGC responses by tectal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 represent the authors' integrated model synthesizing the experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (pharmacology, imaging, electrophysiology, behavior). However, some mechanistic steps involve inference (e.g., sodium channel de-inactivation is inferred from prior literature and the pre-pulse experiments but not directly measured). The model is internally consistent and parsimonious.

results.result: Background and contextual claims about endocannabinoid signaling, CB1R expression and function, chloride transporter regulation, and prior studies in various systems.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C5-C9, C11, C56, C59, C92-C94, C96-C99, C101-C104, C108-C109) are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. They provide necessary context for the study but do not represent novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work based on the claims made.

results.result: The authors claim their work presents a novel mechanism for interaction between glycinergic inhibition and the endocannabinoid system, and is one of the first to suggest a role for tonic GlyR-mediated inhibition in the retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C95 and C100 represent the authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings. The mechanism involving CB1R-mediated regulation of [Cl−]i to modulate tonic glycinergic inhibition and enhance intrinsic excitability does appear novel based on the literature cited. The claim about tonic GlyR inhibition in retina (C100) is appropriately qualified as 'one of the first' rather than claiming absolute priority.

results.result: Speculative claims about the functional significance of the findings, including auto/paracrine AEA signaling, signal-to-noise ratio optimization, and benefits during dark adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C106, and C111 are speculative interpretations of the functional significance of the findings. While plausible and consistent with the data, they are not directly tested. C105 proposes auto/paracrine AEA signaling based on RGC expression of AEA synthetic/degradative enzymes (C103) and the cell-autonomous effects demonstrated.
